newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian parliament debates new cabinet programme.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian parliament debates new cabinet programme.

text.p: Bulgaria's Prime Minister designate Ivan Kostov, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) which won last month's election, on Wednesday presented to parliament his cabinet lineup and main priorities.

"After years of reform imitation and overt asset stripping, our government pledges to haul Bulgaria out of the crisis and bring it up to the standards of other European countries," Kostov told parliament.
Parliament, where the UDF holds a majority 137 of 240 seats, is expected to vote on the appointment of the new cabinet and prime minister later on Wednesday.

Kostov is keeping on five ministers from the interim cabinet, including deputy premier and industry minister Alexander Bozhkov and interior minister Bogomil Bonev who will continue his campaign against crime and high-level corruption.
His cabinet includes Muravei Radev, 50, head of the previous parliament's economic commission, as finance minister, and UDF deputy leader Nadezhda Mihailova as foreign minister.

The main priorities outlined in the UDF programme are carrying out economic reform, footing its social cost, fighting organised crime, opening secret police files of public figures, returning land to pre-communist owners and bringing Bulgaria into the European Union and NATO.
"We need to provide adequate social safety nets for those who will be most affected by pending restructuring of state enterprises," said Kostov.

Introducing an IMF-prescribed currency board system and a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime designed to stabilise the country's shaky banks and volatile currency will be the first task of the new cabinet.
Setting up a Foreign Investment Council and promoting investment opportunities in Bulgaria through road shows will be one of the actions of the new cabinet, said Kostov.
Speeding privatisation, closing inefficient and loss-making state enterprises and selling off state banks to preferably foreign strategic investors by end-1998 are major targets, said Kostov.
Strengthening government institutions and reducing redundant state administration are further aims, he said.
"Our final aim is to bring Bulgaria into the 21st century as a civilised European country."

The UDF has strong support from the small Euroleft coalition which includes prominent Socialist dissidents, and more guarded support from the Union for National Salvation, which includes ethnic Turks and monarchists.

Deputies of the former ruling Socialists, widely blamed by Bulgarians for the country's economic near-collapse, said they would vote against the new cabinet because its programme lacked figures. The Socialists have 58 seats in parliament.
